episodes.title: Episode 1 – Solution Design & Architecture
episodes.intro: Welcome to episode one, Solution Design and Architecture. This domain is seventeen percent of the exam, so it's one of the big ones. Over six parts, we'll go from a vague business request to an architecture you can defend: who does what, which pattern fits, how multi-agent systems stay honest, and how to show the business why it's worth building.

parts.title: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
parts.official_wording: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
parts.architecture_example: "Process insurance claims" becomes four capabilities: field extraction by Claude with a verifier, coverage lookup from the policy database, routing by the rules engine, and a notification drafted by Claude and reviewed by the adjuster.
parts.exam_takeaway: Capability is not feasibility. Gather volume, input size and latency, then give a verdict with its constraints.
parts.narration:
Let's start with the move that comes before any architecture. A partner rarely hands you a clean requirement. They say something like, "we want AI to handle our claims." Your first job is to break that into separate capabilities, and give each one an owner.

There are three owners. Claude takes the language work: reading, summarising, drafting, planning. Existing systems keep anything the partner has already paid to make reliable, like the policy database or the rules engine. Humans keep the judgement calls, the approvals and the exceptions.

To decide where Claude fits, use the four properties. Next-token prediction means Claude is strong on patterns but can be fluently wrong on specifics like dates and amounts. Knowledge means rare or changing facts should come from an external source of truth. Working memory means the context window is a hard edge. And steerability means concrete instructions work, while abstract ones drift.

Finally, never confirm feasibility just because a demo worked. Ask about volume, input size and latency first. Then give one of three verdicts: feasible as scoped, feasible with constraints, or not feasible. And write the constraints into the statement of work.

knowledge_check.question: A sponsor wants feasibility confirmed after one good demo. What comes first?

options.A: Confirm now, because the working demo proved it
options.B: Gather volume, input size and latency
options.C: Build the production system first
options.D: Add a timeline contingency and confirm today

knowledge_check.why: The verdict is only as sound as the constraints gathered before it.

knowledge_check.question: Which owner should calculate refund amounts against contract rates?

options.A: Claude, using the rates it learned in training
options.B: A human analyst, recalculating every claim
options.C: The existing rate engine
options.D: A subagent

knowledge_check.why: Authoritative values and arithmetic belong to deterministic systems.

knowledge_check.question: A design works up to 150 pages, and 8% of documents are longer. What is the verdict?

options.A: Feasible as scoped, since 92% of documents fit
options.C: Feasible with constraints, documented
options.D: Feasible, with long documents revisited after launch

knowledge_check.why: State the verdict plus the boundary condition that makes it true.

parts.title: Design end-to-end architectures
parts.official_wording: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
parts.architecture_example: Invoice processing: OCR and a server-side tenant ID going in, schema extraction with an evaluator pass, validated JSON with low-confidence fields routed to a human queue, and reviewer corrections feeding the golden dataset.
parts.exam_takeaway: A diagram that ends at "response to user" is missing the feedback loop. The loop is how a system notices it's degrading.
parts.narration:
An end-to-end architecture has four stages, and each stage needs its own controls.

At the input, identity comes from your server, not from the user's message. Data is cut down to what the task actually needs. And anything coming in, including retrieved documents, is screened.

Processing is where you choose the pattern and the reference architecture, the model tier and the context strategy.

At the output, there's a contract: a schema, a validation step, output screening, and a confidence score that decides whether a person needs to look first.

And then the stage most diagrams forget: the feedback loop. You log outcomes, like whether the downstream system accepted the result, or a reviewer corrected it. Those signals feed your evals and a governance table with triggers and owners. Without that loop, a system can quietly drift for weeks and nobody notices.

One more thing. Every pipeline needs an exception path. If messy documents travel the same road as clean ones, wrong outputs flow downstream at the same rate as right ones.

knowledge_check.question: Wrong extractions post to the ERP as often as right ones. What's missing?

options.A: A larger, more capable extraction model
options.C: A confidence-based exception path
options.D: A nightly re-run of every document batch

knowledge_check.why: Low-confidence outputs need their own route to human review.

knowledge_check.question: Quality eroded for weeks before anyone noticed. Which stage was missing?

options.A: Input screening for injected content
options.C: Model selection for each pipeline step
options.D: Output schema

knowledge_check.why: Outcome signals and triggers are what detect degradation.

knowledge_check.question: Where does verified user identity come from?

options.A: The user's own message, as they state it
options.B: A role field in the system prompt template
options.C: The server, from authentication
options.D: The model

knowledge_check.why: Self-asserted identity can be faked.

parts.title: Select appropriate architectural patterns
parts.official_wording: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
parts.architecture_example: A disbursement agent's traces showed only four paths. A router with four chains gave the auditor a discrete approval step.
parts.exam_takeaway: If you can write the steps down, write them in code. Use an agent only when the path really can't be listed in advance.
parts.narration:
There are three shapes Claude's involvement can take.

An augmented LLM is a single call. It may use tools or retrieval, but it does one bounded job, and the control flow never branches on what the model decides.

A workflow is a set of steps orchestrated in your own code. You can log it, test it, and point to exactly which step did what.

An agent is different. You give the model a goal and tools, and the model decides its own sequence of steps. The control flow lives inside the model.

Workflows come in five common shapes. Prompt chaining, with checks between steps. Routing, when the categories are clear. Parallelization, either splitting into sections or voting. Orchestrator-workers, when the subtasks can't be known until runtime. And evaluator-optimizer, when you can generate, check against criteria, and refine.

To choose, walk five factors in order: predictability, error cost, observability, latency and cost. The tightest constraint picks the pattern.

And when prompting feels unreliable, don't jump to fine-tuning. Improve the prompt first, then add tools or retrieval, then try a stronger pattern. Fine-tuning comes last, if at all.

knowledge_check.question: Five known email categories with accurate classification. Which pattern fits?

options.A: Autonomous agent
options.C: Multi-agent system
options.D: Fine-tuned model per category

knowledge_check.why: Distinct categories with accurate classification is the routing case.

knowledge_check.question: Which situation justifies an agent?

options.A: The steps are known but there are many of them
options.B: The path depends on what each step uncovers
options.C: The auditor needs to see a named approval step
options.D: Latency is very tight

knowledge_check.why: Agents fit work where the path can't be listed in advance.

knowledge_check.question: Prompting seems unreliable for an extraction task. What comes next?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the extraction examples
options.C: Improve the prompt, then tools, then a stronger pattern
options.D: Use the biggest model and skip the eval set

knowledge_check.why: Fine-tuning is the last step in the progression.

parts.title: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
parts.official_wording: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
parts.architecture_example: A 50-section contract review reported "48 reviewed, 3 flagged" because two subagents silently returned nothing. A coverage check would have flagged the gap.
parts.exam_takeaway: Reconcile coverage, protect orchestrator state, and use the fewest agents that meet the requirement.
parts.narration:
Some work is too large or too varied for one agent to hold in a single context. That's where multi-agent systems come in.

The orchestrator owns the goal. It breaks the work apart, delegates and synthesises, but it doesn't do the sub-tasks itself. Subagents each own one scoped piece, in their own clean context.

The most common shape is fan-out: split a big item into independent units, run one subagent per unit in parallel, then combine the results.

Here's the key design insight. Failure is asymmetric. If a subagent fails, that's usually recoverable: retry it, re-route it, or flag the gap. If the orchestrator fails, the whole run can be lost. So checkpoint the orchestrator's state, and make subagent work safe to retry.

The most dangerous failure is a silent one. The summary looks complete, but some units never came back. The fix is a coverage check: results returned must equal units dispatched.

Also design how conflicts get resolved, give every agent the same trace ID, and gate any irreversible action behind a person. Anthropic's own research system found multi-agent setups use roughly fifteen times the tokens of chat, so use them only when the work truly needs them.

knowledge_check.question: Two subagents timed out and the summary still looked complete. What's the fix?

options.A: A more capable model for the orchestrator
options.C: A coverage check at synthesis
options.D: Running every section sequentially instead

knowledge_check.why: Results returned must equal units dispatched.

knowledge_check.question: Which failure is usually unrecoverable?

options.A: A subagent returning a malformed result
options.C: The orchestrator losing its state
options.D: A subagent timeout

knowledge_check.why: The orchestrator holds the goal and the synthesis, so protect it.

knowledge_check.question: When is multi-agent a poor fit?

options.A: The work is far larger than one context
options.C: The steps depend heavily on each other
options.D: Breadth-first research across many sources

knowledge_check.why: Heavy dependencies and shared context don't suit multi-agent.

parts.title: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
parts.official_wording: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
parts.architecture_example: Law-firm contract review: iManage fetches documents, Claude compares clauses against the playbook section by section in parallel, and the senior associate signs off.
parts.exam_takeaway: Decompose by owner first, then by step. Gate between steps, and parallelise only what is truly independent.
parts.narration:
Decomposition happens at three levels.

The first is ownership: Claude, systems or humans. You justify each assignment with three questions. Can a wrong call be undone? What does a wrong call cost? And who has to answer for it? That's reversibility, stakes and accountability. The result is a delegation map, where some work is Claude's, some stays human, and some is collaborative, with Claude drafting and a person deciding.

The second level is capabilities. Turn the business goal into a list of named things the system must do, so each one can get the right owner.

The third level is the work itself. Chain steps with checks between them. Fan out independent units. And when an input is bigger than the context window, decompose the input itself, by section, with a synthesis step and a coverage check at the end.

One trap to avoid: only parallelise units that are truly independent. If the executive summary depends on three sections, those sections can run in parallel, but the summary has to wait for them.

knowledge_check.question: Which three criteria justify a delegation decision?

options.A: Speed, cost and the size of the model
options.C: Volume, latency and token consumption
options.D: Accuracy, fluency, tone

knowledge_check.why: These decide whether Claude should own a decision.

knowledge_check.question: Three independent sections plus a summary that depends on them. What's the plan?

options.A: Run all four parts in parallel at once
options.C: Sections in parallel, then a gated summary
options.D: Chain all four parts with no checks between

knowledge_check.why: Parallelise only the independent units.

knowledge_check.question: The input is larger than the context window. Which approach fits?

options.A: Truncate the input to what fits in the window
options.B: Summarise the whole input in one model call first
options.C: Split by section, extract, then synthesise with a coverage check
options.D: Use the full input and accept any truncation

knowledge_check.why: Decompose the input when it exceeds working memory.

parts.title: Align solutions to business value pillars
parts.official_wording: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
parts.architecture_example: Claims triage drops from 40 to 15 analyst minutes, because review is still required. Net value is the hours saved minus the monthly run cost from sizing, with payback shown at lower volume too.
parts.exam_takeaway: Technical metrics show the system runs. A before-and-after business metric shows it's worth expanding.
parts.narration:
A feasible design isn't automatically a worthwhile one. Here's how to make the business case.

There are five value pillars. Efficiency means the same work, faster or cheaper. Transformation means work that wasn't possible before, like reviewing every case instead of a small sample. Productivity means more output from the same people. Cost means the run cost of the solution itself. And performance SLAs are the service levels the deployment has to hold.

Then build the ROI in four steps. First, measure today's baseline in a unit the business already tracks, using their own data, not intuition. Second, project the new state in the same unit, and remember: if a person still reviews some outputs, that time is still a cost. Third, subtract the monthly run cost, taken from your sizing distribution, not an average. Fourth, give a payback period, and show how it moves if volume or gains come in lower.

When you close the engagement, the outcome document needs the business metric before and after, the control that makes that comparison auditable, and an owner who keeps measuring it.

knowledge_check.question: A deployment lets compliance review every communication instead of five percent. Which pillar?

options.A: Efficiency
options.C: Cost
options.D: Performance SLA

knowledge_check.why: Work that wasn't feasible before is transformation.

knowledge_check.question: The business case assumes zero analyst hours, but twenty percent of items go to review. What's the flaw?

options.A: Nothing; the projection is reasonable
options.B: It overstates value by ignoring review effort
options.C: It should count tokens saved rather than hours
options.D: Review time belongs in the one-off build cost

knowledge_check.why: Net human review effort out of the projected gain.

knowledge_check.question: What does a CFO need from an outcome document?

options.A: Request volume, latency and the error rate
options.B: The model tier used at each pipeline step
options.C: Business metric before and after, an auditable control, and an owner
options.D: The prompts used, so the CFO sees how it works

knowledge_check.why: That's what justifies expansion.

episodes.title: Episode 2 – Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
episodes.intro: Episode two covers models, prompting and context engineering, thirteen percent of the exam. Five parts: choosing a model tier, designing prompts as reusable assets, picking the right technique, managing the context window, and reusing prompts through caching and Skills.

parts.title: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
parts.official_wording: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
parts.architecture_example: A Sonnet to Haiku migration averaged 0.86, but two document types fell below the pre-set 0.85 floor. Those two stayed on Sonnet and the rest moved to Haiku.
parts.exam_takeaway: Start with Sonnet. Every move up or down is a release, gated by an eval with a threshold you set in advance.
parts.narration:
The Claude family has three tiers. Opus is the most capable, Sonnet balances capability, speed and cost, and Haiku is the fastest and cheapest.

The default starting point is Sonnet. Move up to Opus only when an eval shows Sonnet misses your quality bar. Move down to Haiku only when an eval confirms the quality trade-off is acceptable.

Treat every model change as a release. You need a representative test set, a grading function, and a pass threshold, and you set that threshold before you run anything. Look at scores per category, not just the average. A downgrade can look fine on average while failing badly on two document types. That's when a partial migration makes sense.

Not every step needs the same model. Classification might run on Haiku, summarisation on Sonnet, and only the final answer on Opus.

Extended thinking is a cost and latency trade-off. Thinking tokens are billed as output, so turn it on only when an eval shows an accuracy gap that prompt work couldn't close.

And pin your model versions, so a silent roll-forward never surprises an auditor.

knowledge_check.question: Which tier is the recommended default for a new build?

options.A: Sonnet
options.C: Haiku
options.D: Whatever the last project used

knowledge_check.why: Start with Sonnet and move only on eval evidence.

knowledge_check.question: When should the rollback threshold be set?

options.A: After seeing the results
options.C: After launch
options.D: Never

knowledge_check.why: Setting it afterwards just writes acceptance criteria to fit the data.

knowledge_check.question: When is extended thinking justified?

options.A: Always, because extra reasoning can't hurt quality
options.B: On every routing classifier to improve its accuracy
options.C: When an eval shows an accuracy gap after prompt work
options.D: Whenever the latency budget has room to spare

knowledge_check.why: It adds billed tokens and latency on every call.

parts.title: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
parts.official_wording: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
parts.architecture_example: A support-reply template caches role, tone, contract and a no-refund-promise rule, with slots only for the ticket and the manual section. The output contract has no field where a commitment could go.
parts.exam_takeaway: A system prompt reused at scale is an asset you design. Make the safe path the default path, and remember that a prompt alone isn't enforcement.
parts.narration:
At enterprise scale, a system prompt isn't a sentence you type. It's an asset hundreds of requests a day depend on, so it needs structure.

State the role and scope: what's in bounds and what's out. List the constraints: what Claude must always do and must never do. And define the output contract, the exact shape the response has to take.

A template takes that further. It has fixed scaffolding that carries the safety and consistency guarantees, plus slots for the content that changes. Filling a slot should never be able to remove a constraint. The person using the template supplies the variable content and inherits the guardrails automatically.

The skill here is called Description: telling the model precisely what you want. The failure it prevents is underspecification. Wherever the prompt is silent, the model fills the gap, differently each time. So read your prompt asking, for each requirement, is this actually stated, or am I just hoping for it?

Finally, put important guardrails into the structure of the output, not just the role text, and back them with runtime screening. A rule stated in prose can be drifted past.

knowledge_check.question: Outputs vary in structure and miss required citations. What's missing?

options.A: A longer list of adjectives describing tone
options.B: A higher temperature for more natural variety
options.C: An output contract and explicit constraints
options.D: A larger model that infers the structure itself

knowledge_check.why: Underspecified prompts let the model improvise.

knowledge_check.question: What should a template's fixed scaffolding guarantee?

options.A: That filling slots can't remove constraints
options.C: Faster responses for users
options.D: Fewer tokens in each prompt

knowledge_check.why: The safe path should be the default path.

knowledge_check.question: How do you enforce "never promise refunds" most robustly?

options.A: Repeat the rule several times in the role text
options.B: Move the rule to the very end of the prompt
options.C: Build it into the output contract and add screening
options.D: Raise max_tokens so every rule can be followed

knowledge_check.why: Structural constraints are harder to drift past than prose.

parts.title: Apply prompt engineering techniques
parts.official_wording: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
parts.architecture_example: A 12-category classifier confused two categories zero-shot. Two balanced examples per confusable pair fixed it, while chain-of-thought added latency for no gain.
parts.exam_takeaway: Use the lightest technique that meets the requirement. Each step adds tokens and latency.
parts.narration:
There are three core techniques, and you should reach for them in order.

Zero-shot is instruction only. Try it first for any well-specified task.

Few-shot adds a handful of input and output examples. Use it when the format or the judgement is easier to show than to describe. But keep the examples balanced across the cases the system will really see. If every example shows the same kind of answer, you've built bias into the prompt. The same goes for leading phrasing, like "confirm this applicant qualifies".

Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering. It helps with multi-step logic, but it's a tax on every call, so don't use it where it doesn't move accuracy.

And for precise arithmetic, like totals with discounts and tax, don't rely on reasoning at all. Let code execution or a deterministic service own the number.

One more point. Prompts and models ship as a pair. A more capable model often needs less scaffolding, so when you change tiers, re-tune the prompt and evaluate the pairing.

knowledge_check.question: Which technique should you try first on a well-specified task?

options.A: Chain-of-thought
options.C: Fine-tuning
options.D: Zero-shot

knowledge_check.why: Start light and escalate only on evidence.

knowledge_check.question: The format is hard to describe but easy to recognise. Which technique fits?

options.A: Chain-of-thought reasoning
options.C: A lower temperature setting
options.D: A larger max_tokens value

knowledge_check.why: Show, don't tell.

knowledge_check.question: Pricing totals with tax are often wrong. What's the best fix?

options.A: Tell the model to double-check its arithmetic
options.B: Add examples showing correctly computed totals
options.C: Let code or a pricing service compute the totals
options.D: Switch to a bigger model that does better maths

knowledge_check.why: Deterministic computation should own the number.

parts.title: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
parts.official_wording: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
parts.architecture_example: A legal chat started truncating late in sessions. Compacting old turns while keeping clause IDs, retrieving clauses on demand, and caching the policy prefix fixed it.
parts.exam_takeaway: Count tokens, budget with margin, and remember the model has no memory between calls unless your application provides it.
parts.narration:
The context window is the model's working memory, and it has a hard edge. Inside it, everything is available. Outside it, nothing exists.

There are two different ways to hit that edge, so know them apart. If the request itself is too big, the API rejects it before generation. Too many tokens gives a four hundred error. Too many bytes gives a four thirteen. But if the request fits and the response runs into the ceiling while it's generating, you get truncated output with a context-window stop reason.

Don't estimate tokens from characters. Measure them, using the usage field on every response and the token-counting API before you send. Then budget for the largest realistic conversation, plus retrieved context, plus the system prompt, plus scratch space, plus margin. The window is a ceiling, not a target.

Watch the distribution too. Most requests may be short, but a tail of long ones can drive most of your cost.

And keep your terms straight. Retrieval brings knowledge in. Live state comes through tools. And memory between sessions isn't a model feature. Your application stores it and passes it back in.

knowledge_check.question: A request returns a 400 saying the prompt is too long. What happened?

options.A: Generation hit the context ceiling midway through
options.B: It was rejected before generation for too many tokens
options.C: A transient server error worth retrying with backoff
options.D: The request body exceeded the API's byte limit

knowledge_check.why: Oversized-token requests are rejected with a 400; the byte limit gives 413.

knowledge_check.question: How should you size context?

options.A: Four characters per token, designed to 95 percent
options.B: Measure with usage and token counting, and leave margin
options.C: Watch the monthly bill and adjust from there
options.D: Use the biggest window available and stop worrying

knowledge_check.why: Measure, and treat the window as a ceiling.

knowledge_check.question: The assistant greets returning users by name. Why?

options.A: The model has native memory of past users
options.B: The model was fine-tuned on each returning user
options.C: Prompt caching stores user preferences between sessions
options.D: The application stores state and passes it back

knowledge_check.why: Continuity is managed by the application.

parts.title: Implement prompt reuse strategies
parts.official_wording: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
key_concepts: container.skills and the Code Execution Tool
parts.architecture_example: A team's cache never hit because the per-request document came before the fixed instructions. Reordering fixed it.
parts.exam_takeaway: Put fixed content first and cache it. Package repeatable, distributed, governed procedures as versioned Skills.
parts.narration:
When the same long instructions go out on every request, prompt caching is your biggest lever. The cache works on a stable prefix, so order matters. Put the fixed content first, mark a breakpoint, and put the per-request content after it. If dynamic content comes first, the prefix changes every time and the cache never hits.

Caching isn't free. Writing to the cache costs more than normal input, and entries expire. The default lifetime is five minutes, so a prompt called a few times a month may never earn back the write. Model the economics: how often it's called, how big the prefix is, and how often it changes.

For reuse across a team, you have two options. A modular prompt library is a set of fragments engineers assemble in their own code. It's flexible and lightweight. A Skill is a versioned, self-contained unit that packages a procedure, its instructions and any scripts, so it can be governed and rolled back.

On the API, Skills attach to requests and need the Code Execution Tool, which brings a sandboxed execution dependency. And Skills load progressively: metadata first, full content only when needed.

knowledge_check.question: Caching is enabled but there are no savings. What's the likely cause?

options.A: The cache TTL is set too short for the traffic
options.B: Dynamic content comes before the fixed prefix
options.C: The model tier is too small to use caching
options.D: Outputs are too long for the cache to apply

knowledge_check.why: The cache matches a stable prefix.

knowledge_check.question: A procedure runs the same way across many teams and needs rollback. Which packaging?

options.A: A versioned Skill
options.B: Templates pasted into each team's prompts
options.C: A wiki page describing the procedure
options.D: A modular prompt library assembled per use

knowledge_check.why: Repeatable, distributed and governed points to a Skill.

knowledge_check.question: When might caching cost more than it saves?

options.A: A long prefix that's called constantly
options.B: A static policy document that's called often
options.C: A small prefix called a few times a month
options.D: A stable system prompt reused all day

knowledge_check.why: Write overhead isn't recovered at low frequency.

episodes.title: Episode 3 – Integration
episodes.intro: Episode three is Integration, the biggest domain on the exam at nineteen percent. Eight parts: trimming excess tools, closing identity gaps, justifying accuracy and latency trade-offs, monitoring at scale, designing retrieval pipelines, matching retrieval to the data, choosing connection protocols, and progressive versus monolithic context.

parts.title: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
parts.official_wording: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
key_concepts: deferral is not a permission control
parts.architecture_example: A support agent could read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete accounts, but staff only read and draft. Remove the refund and delete tools.
parts.exam_takeaway: If a role doesn't need a capability, remove it. Don't log it, confirm it or instruct around it.
parts.narration:
Every tool you connect to Claude is two things at once: an attack surface and a cost. Capability bloat is when an agent holds more tools or permissions than its task needs.

So audit the tool set the way you'd audit permissions. For each tool, ask: is this essential to the task, or just convenient? If it's out of scope, remove it, and write down why.

The exam loves one particular trap here. A plausible answer adds logging to a dangerous tool, or a confirmation prompt, or a system-prompt rule saying "never use this". Those are compensating controls. The privilege is still there. The strongest answer removes the capability the role doesn't need.

In multi-agent systems, scope each subagent's tools to its own job. A subagent that only reads and reports findings shouldn't inherit the orchestrator's ability to file documents or send notifications. That's the trust hierarchy.

And one subtle point: tool search and deferred loading reduce how much of your context window tool definitions take up. They don't reduce what the agent is allowed to call.

knowledge_check.question: Staff only read and draft, but the agent can also delete accounts. Best change?

options.A: Log deletions
options.C: Remove the delete tool
options.D: Use a larger model

knowledge_check.why: Least privilege removes the capability at its source.

knowledge_check.question: Do deferred tools reduce an agent's permissions?

options.A: Yes, deferred tools can no longer be called
options.B: Yes, but only for tools with side effects
options.C: Only when the tools are accessed through the API
options.D: No, they only change what enters context

knowledge_check.why: A deferred tool can still be found and called.

knowledge_check.question: Subagents inherit every orchestrator tool. What's the fix?

options.A: Scope each subagent's tools to its task
options.B: Ask subagents to justify any write action
options.C: Move the shared tools onto an MCP server
options.D: Upgrade each subagent to a stronger model

knowledge_check.why: This sets up a trust hierarchy.

parts.title: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements
parts.official_wording: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
key_concepts: the Claude layer inherits the existing authorization model
parts.architecture_example: A legal search tool ran on an all-access service account while the system prompt said "only use permitted documents". The fix: the tool enforces the user's matter-level permissions.
parts.exam_takeaway: Who you are comes from authentication, through the server. What you may do is enforced by deterministic code, never by a prompt.
parts.narration:
Security gaps in Claude integrations usually come from three places.

The first is identity. If a user can type "I'm a regional controller" and unlock data, you have a spoofing gap. Identity and role must come from your authentication layer, and your server injects them into the system prompt. Never trust what the user claims in their message.

The second is authorization. The Claude layer must follow the same access model as the systems underneath it. If your search tool runs on an account that can see every record, a polite instruction in the prompt doesn't help. The tool itself must query as the verified user. And any action with side effects, like booking, refunding or sending, goes through a deterministic check of identity, action and scope.

The third is multi-tenancy. One shared API key means one tenant's spike can trip the limit for everyone, and you can't tell who caused it. Use a separate key per tenant.

For remote MCP servers holding non-public data, the specification treats the server as an OAuth 2.1 resource server. It publishes its metadata, and clients send an access token on every request, instead of sharing a static secret.

knowledge_check.question: Users unlock reports by stating their role in chat. What's the gap?

options.A: The system prompt is too short to list every role
options.B: The prompt lacks few-shot examples for each role
options.C: Self-asserted identity instead of server-side injection
options.D: The model tier is too small to spot false claims

knowledge_check.why: Identity must come from authentication, injected by the server.

knowledge_check.question: Sixty tenants share one API key and a spike degrades everyone. What's the fix?

options.A: A separate key per tenant
options.C: Batch API
options.D: Put tenant_id in the prompt

knowledge_check.why: Per-tenant keys give attribution and isolation.

knowledge_check.question: How should a protected remote MCP server authorise clients?

options.A: With a shared secret stored in each client's config
options.B: As an OAuth 2.1 resource server with access tokens
options.C: By VPN restriction alone, with no user-level checks
options.D: By having each client pass the username in tool calls

knowledge_check.why: This follows the MCP authorization specification.

parts.title: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
parts.official_wording: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
key_concepts: Tier, thinking, context, retrieval and caching as levers
parts.architecture_example: Extended thinking on a routing classifier added latency with no accuracy gain. Turning it off and moving that step to Haiku met the SLA.
parts.exam_takeaway: Name the constraint with the least margin and the lever that moves it, and justify the change with an eval.
parts.narration:
Every configuration choice trades accuracy against latency and cost. The levers are model tier, extended thinking, how much context you send, how you retrieve, the output cap, and caching.

Start by stating three numbers that come from the business: the accuracy bar, the latency budget, and the cost ceiling. For latency, design against p95, the time ninety-five percent of requests finish within. The median hides the slow tail, and the slow tail is what breaks SLAs.

Then find the binding constraint, the one with the least margin. If latency is binding, tier and thinking are your strongest levers. If cost is binding, tier and context strategy matter most.

Change one lever at a time, and measure each change against your eval. A common win is per-step tiering: a cheap model for routing, a mid tier for summarising, and the top tier only where the eval says it earns its place.

On retrieval, smaller chunks and hybrid indexes tend to raise quality and latency together. Large dense-only chunks are faster, but they miss exact-match queries like product codes.

knowledge_check.question: Users complain about slowness, but median latency looks fine. What should you check?

options.A: p95 latency
options.C: Error rate
options.D: Token count

knowledge_check.why: SLA breaches live in the slow tail.

knowledge_check.question: Cost is double the ceiling and latency has margin. Which levers matter most?

options.A: Extended thinking only
options.C: Adding hybrid retrieval
options.D: Output length on the final step

knowledge_check.why: These move cost most, validated by eval.

knowledge_check.question: What justifies a configuration decision?

options.A: A successful live demo
options.C: An eval against the stated thresholds
options.D: Published vendor benchmark results

knowledge_check.why: Measured evidence makes a choice defensible.

parts.title: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
parts.official_wording: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
key_concepts: tracing, aggregation, anomaly detection, change attribution
parts.architecture_example: Dashboards were green while a small share of long documents consumed most of the budget. Breaking cost down by input-length bucket exposed it.
parts.exam_takeaway: LLMs fail quietly. Instrument outcomes, break metrics down per request, and attribute a change before you fix it.
parts.narration:
Traditional systems crash when something goes wrong. LLM systems usually don't. They give an answer that's subtly wrong, with normal latency and no error. So error-rate dashboards alone will miss most problems.

On every request, log four things. The request: model version, input tokens, prompt identifier. The response: output tokens, latency, stop reason. The context: user role, session, whether the cache was hit. And the outcome: did the downstream system accept the result, or was it rejected or corrected?

Then monitor in four layers. Tracing for every request, including tool calls. Aggregation into cost, p50 and p95 latency, task success and error types, broken down per request, because averages hide the expensive tail. Anomaly detection, with alerts on spikes plus periodic comparison for slow drift. And change attribution, which separates model drift, data drift and a model version update, because each one has a different fix.

For multi-agent systems, use one shared trace ID across every agent. And for agents that take actions, check that every action is written to an audit log. An action that isn't logged is one a security reviewer can't approve.

knowledge_check.question: Error rate is low, yet escalations are rising. What's missing?

options.A: A higher error-rate alert threshold
options.C: Adding p50 latency to the dashboards
options.D: Verbose logging of raw prompts and PII

knowledge_check.why: Quality failures don't show up as errors.

knowledge_check.question: You can't link subagent failures to their runs. What should you add?

options.A: Per-agent dashboards
options.C: A bigger orchestrator
options.D: A shared trace ID

knowledge_check.why: One ID makes the whole run reconstructable.

knowledge_check.question: Which three causes does change attribution separate?

options.A: Model drift, data drift, model update
options.C: Prompts, tools and individual users
options.D: Input size, output size and context

knowledge_check.why: Each has a different fix.

parts.title: Design a RAG pipeline with chunking and indexing strategies
parts.official_wording: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
parts.architecture_example: Policy answers cited an exclusion clause without the heading that limited it to commercial policies. Hierarchical chunking kept section context with each clause.
parts.exam_takeaway: Chunk by the shape of the source, index by the shape of the queries, and measure retrieval on its own.
parts.narration:
A retrieval pipeline makes two key decisions: how you chunk the corpus, and how you index it.

Choose chunking by the structure of the source. Fixed-size chunks with overlap suit uniform, unstructured text. Semantic chunking splits on meaning, so each chunk can stand on its own. Hierarchical chunking keeps sections and subsections together. That's what you want for contracts, manuals and policies, where a heading changes what a clause means.

Choose indexing by how people ask. Dense embeddings match meaning, which is great for paraphrased questions. Sparse keyword search, like BM25, matches exact tokens: part numbers, error codes, statute citations. Most production systems see both kinds of query, so hybrid is the common answer. Merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, a low-tuning default.

Every choice trades retrieval quality against latency and maintenance. And retrieval quality doesn't show in the output. A confident answer built on the wrong chunk looks exactly like a right one. So measure retrieval precision and recall against a labelled set, and keep measuring as the corpus grows.

knowledge_check.question: Users search by part number and by description. Which index fits?

options.A: Dense embeddings only
options.C: Hybrid with reciprocal rank fusion
options.D: No index, just a long prompt

knowledge_check.why: Mixed query patterns call for hybrid.

knowledge_check.question: Clauses lose the context of their section heading. Which chunking fits?

options.A: Hierarchical
options.C: Larger top-k
options.D: A bigger embedding model

knowledge_check.why: Preserve document structure.

knowledge_check.question: Answers turn confidently wrong after a document refresh. Where do you look first?

options.A: Silently changed model weights
options.B: A temperature that is set too low
options.C: A context window that has shrunk
options.D: Retrieval and indexing

knowledge_check.why: For example, mismatched embeddings or a broken re-index.

parts.title: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
parts.official_wording: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
key_concepts: tool calls for systems of record
monolithic prefix for small stable content
parts.architecture_example: "Where's my order?" returned two stale chunks and a confident wrong answer, while an order-status API sat unused.
parts.exam_takeaway: If it was true yesterday and will be true tomorrow, retrieve it. If its value changes on its own, call the system that owns it.
parts.narration:
Here's the most common reference-architecture mistake: using retrieval where a tool call belongs.

Retrieval is built for stable knowledge: FAQs, manuals, policies, things that stay true between index refreshes. Live state is different. Order status, inventory and account balances are owned by a system of record and change independently. If you index snapshots of live state, the retriever returns whichever stale snapshot looks most similar, and the model answers confidently. No error, normal latency, wrong answer.

A shorter refresh interval won't fix this, and neither will a higher similarity threshold or a better embedding model. Similarity isn't truth. The fix is a tool call to the system that owns the data.

So classify each kind of data. Stable reference content goes through retrieval, or a cached prefix if it's small and always needed. Live state comes from the system of record. Precise numbers come from deterministic computation.

And when a question needs synthesis across many documents, top-k chunks often miss the pattern. Break it into per-document extraction, then synthesise over the structured findings.

knowledge_check.question: Answers about order status contradict the database. What's the fix?

options.A: An hourly refresh
options.C: A higher similarity threshold
options.D: Better embeddings

knowledge_check.why: Live state belongs to the system of record.

knowledge_check.question: Where should a small, stable policy needed on every call go?

options.A: A cached monolithic prefix
options.C: Fine-tuning on the policy
options.D: A tool call on every request

knowledge_check.why: There's no need to pay retrieval overhead for it.

knowledge_check.question: Cross-document synthesis keeps missing patterns. What should you do?

options.A: Raise top-k to fifty and let the model synthesise
options.B: Switch to sparse-only retrieval for exact matches
options.C: Answer the synthesis from the model's own memory
options.D: Extract per document, then synthesise

knowledge_check.why: Retrieval scores chunks independently, so synthesis needs structure.

parts.title: Evaluate connection protocols and select the integration mechanism
parts.official_wording: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
parts.architecture_example: A bank proposed Claude Code on branch laptops with MCP servers. The better design was a custom web app on the API with SSO, deterministic compliance code and server-side audit.
parts.exam_takeaway: The entry point follows the user and the work. Use MCP only when two or more clients reuse the same tools.
parts.narration:
Choosing how Claude connects is about matching the mechanism to the job.

The direct API is the foundation layer, giving you full control and full responsibility. The SDKs offer the same capability in language-native code, and they're the default for embedding Claude in a product.

MCP is a protocol for sharing tools across clients. Build a server once, and Claude.ai, Claude Code and your internal app can all use it. If only one product will ever use those tools, MCP just adds overhead. MCP and tool use aren't really alternatives, either. MCP servers expose tools that clients call through tool use.

The Agent SDK runs a managed agent loop, the same one behind Claude Code, inside your own application. Pick it when Claude needs to act across several turns in your product and you don't want to build the loop yourself.

Claude Code itself is for developers doing engineering work. It isn't a backend for operational staff or multi-tenant products.

Agent-to-agent protocols cover delegating to agents you don't own, possibly on other frameworks. Anthropic's documentation doesn't address them directly, so treat this as an inferred principle.

knowledge_check.question: Claude.ai, Claude Code and an internal app all need the same Jira tools. Which mechanism?

options.A: Separate integrations
options.C: A static prompt
options.D: One MCP server

knowledge_check.why: MCP shares one tool surface across clients.

knowledge_check.question: An agent embedded in your web app must act over several turns. Which interface?

options.A: Agent SDK
options.C: A single SDK call
options.D: MCP as the loop

knowledge_check.why: The Agent SDK provides the managed loop.

knowledge_check.question: Branch staff need an operations assistant. Which entry point is wrong?

options.A: A custom web app on the API behind SSO
options.C: An SDK-based app integrated with SSO
options.D: An internal portal

knowledge_check.why: Claude Code is for developers, not operational staff.

parts.title: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
parts.official_wording: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
parts.architecture_example: An agent with 12 MCP servers and 350 tools deferred the long tail with tool search and kept its five hottest tools loaded, freeing context before any work began.
parts.exam_takeaway: Load what's needed at the start, carry forward what's recent, fetch the rest on demand, and compress what's old.
parts.narration:
A context strategy decides how information reaches the model on each call. It sits on a spectrum.

Monolithic means loading everything at once. It suits bounded tasks with stable, cacheable prefixes. But in long conversations or agent loops, context piles up turn after turn, cost grows, and eventually you hit the window's edge.

Progressive means carrying forward only what the next step needs. It's the right default for most production work.

Two more strategies sit in between. Retrieval fetches knowledge just in time. Compaction summarises older material so long sessions can keep going, but it can drop exact identifiers and numbers, so preserve those.

Real systems combine all four. A coding agent loads a small stable prefix, carries recent tool results forward, retrieves files when it needs them, and compacts early exploration.

Progressive discovery applies to tools and Skills as well. With the tool search tool, you mark rarely used tools as deferred, and Claude loads them only when it finds it needs them. You still send every definition, and you keep your three to five most-used tools loaded. Skills work the same way: metadata first, full content on demand.

knowledge_check.question: Cost per turn keeps growing in a long agent session. What's the best strategy?

options.A: Move to a much larger context window
options.B: Clear the whole history every ten turns
options.C: Load the entire repository at session start
options.D: Cached prefix, recent state, retrieval and compaction

knowledge_check.why: Combine strategies to control growth.

knowledge_check.question: With tool search, what does defer_loading control?

options.A: Which tool definitions are sent
options.C: Tool permissions
options.D: Tool pricing

knowledge_check.why: Full definitions are still sent with the request.

knowledge_check.question: Which tools should stay non-deferred?

options.A: The most frequently used few
options.C: The tool search tool should be deferred
options.D: Every side-effecting tool

knowledge_check.why: This avoids a search step on most turns.

episodes.title: Episode 4 – Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
episodes.intro: Episode four, Evaluation, Testing and Optimization, is sixteen percent of the exam. Six parts: defining metrics, building eval sets, running real experiments, diagnosing failures, optimising cost and latency, and monitoring performance over time.

parts.title: Define evaluation metrics
parts.official_wording: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
parts.architecture_example: An insurer's framework: exact match on structured fields, p95 under target, cost per claim under the ceiling, no auto-denials, and a code scan for data leaking across claimants.
parts.exam_takeaway: If you can't write an eval for a behaviour, you can't verify it. Thresholds come from the business, not from the prototype.
parts.narration:
"Summarise claims accurately" isn't a metric. To make it one, name the specific behaviour, like extracting the claimant, the policy number, the loss amount and the date. Then set a threshold, and that threshold comes from the business requirement, not from whatever your first prototype happened to score.

Next, list the failure modes: a made-up claim number, a missing date, a value taken from the wrong claim. Each failure mode becomes a category in your dataset. And include adversarial inputs, like handwriting, missing fields and strange layouts. A clean-only dataset predicts nothing about production.

The exam frames metrics in five dimensions: accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security. Most of these can be checked in code. Is the field right? Is p95 under target? Is cost under the ceiling? Was a denial issued? Did any other claimant's identifier appear in this summary? Those are all deterministic checks.

Some safety qualities, like whether a summary is faithful to its source, need interpretation, and that's where a calibrated judge comes in.

knowledge_check.question: Where should an eval threshold come from?

options.A: The score the first prototype achieved
options.C: A competitor's published accuracy claim
options.D: Whatever production shows after launch

knowledge_check.why: Thresholds are acceptance criteria set before building.

knowledge_check.question: Which method fits "never leak another claimant's data"?

options.A: A code-based scan for foreign identifiers
options.B: An LLM judge's privacy score out of ten
options.C: Monthly sampling by the privacy team
options.D: The rate of user complaints about privacy

knowledge_check.why: It's a deterministic property.

knowledge_check.question: The dataset contains only clean forms. What do you add?

options.A: Many more clean forms for statistical power
options.B: A stricter accuracy threshold on clean data
options.C: A more capable judge model for scoring
options.D: Edge cases and adversarial categories

knowledge_check.why: Representative data makes scores meaningful.

parts.title: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
parts.official_wording: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
key_concepts: judge calibration with a different grader model
parts.architecture_example: A summarisation eval kept passing after a prompt change because its dataset predated the change, while production truncated multi-clause sentences.
parts.exam_takeaway: Use code where you can, a calibrated judge where you must, and humans as the last resort. Refresh the dataset every time behaviour changes.
parts.narration:
An eval workflow runs in five stages. Define the task and its pass criteria. Build a golden dataset that's representative, with edge cases. Run automated checks. Score interpretive behaviours with a judge. Then read the results by category, not just as one number.

Choosing how to grade follows a ladder. First, code: schema checks, exact matches, length. It's fast, cheap and never drifts. Second, a model as judge, for things like tone or faithfulness. Make it rigorous with a detailed rubric, a small fixed set of verdicts, reasoning alongside each score, and calibration against human-labelled examples. Use a different model from the one being graded, to avoid self-preference. Third, and last, human review, for novel or high-stakes behaviour, and to calibrate the judge.

Two more rules. Favour volume over perfection: two thousand cheap, automatic cases catch more regressions than forty perfect ones, and they can run on every change. And conversations need multi-turn evals that score whole transcripts.

Finally, the riskiest moment is when an eval exists but is out of date. Every time the prompt or model changes, update the dataset to match.

knowledge_check.question: A judge's scores disagree with experts, and it grades its own model's outputs. What's the fix?

options.A: A finer scale, from 1 to 100
options.B: Average two runs of the same judge
options.C: A rubric, calibration and a different grader model
options.D: A larger model from the same family as the generator

knowledge_check.why: Calibration and avoiding self-preference make judges trustworthy.

knowledge_check.question: Users say the chatbot forgets earlier details. Which eval is missing?

options.A: Multi-turn
options.C: Single-turn adversarial
options.D: Cost

knowledge_check.why: Conversation behaviour needs conversation-level evals.

knowledge_check.question: Forty perfect cases or two thousand automatic ones?

options.A: Forty
options.C: Wait for production
options.D: Two thousand

knowledge_check.why: Broad, cheap coverage catches more regressions.

parts.title: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
parts.official_wording: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
parts.architecture_example: Fifty sessions per arm showed 68 vs. 62 percent and the team shipped. It settled at 61. The test was underpowered, the input mix differed, and the metric was picked after the fact.
parts.exam_takeaway: Write the hypothesis, the primary metric and the sample size before day one. Use shadow testing when exposing users isn't acceptable.
parts.narration:
Experiments on LLM systems need more discipline than usual, because outputs are noisy.

Start with a hypothesis that's specific and falsifiable. Something like: "this instruction change will raise task success by at least five percent, without worsening p95 latency." Choose the primary metric before you start. If you pick it after seeing the results, you can always find one that moved.

Assign users or sessions randomly, and keep the assignment sticky. If one arm happens to get simpler queries, an apparent win may just reflect the input mix. Calculate your sample size from the effect you need to detect. LLM variance is high, so you usually need hundreds of samples, not fifty.

When results come in, ask two questions. Is the effect big enough to be worth maintaining a new version? And did anything else get worse, like cost or latency? Significant isn't the same as worth shipping.

When exposing users to an untested change isn't acceptable, as in many regulated settings, use shadow testing. The new version runs on copied live traffic, users still get the current version, and you score the shadow outputs offline.

knowledge_check.question: A test assigned traffic by support queue. What's the problem?

options.A: The sample was too large
options.C: The wrong metric
options.D: No caching

knowledge_check.why: The groups aren't comparable.

knowledge_check.question: Policy forbids exposing clinicians to untested outputs. Which approach?

options.A: Shadow testing
options.C: A single-ward canary
options.D: Synthetic data only

knowledge_check.why: Shadow testing validates on real traffic without any exposure.

knowledge_check.question: Plus three percent success, plus thirty percent cost, and significant. What now?

options.A: Ship it, since the result is significant
options.B: Discard it, since any cost increase is bad
options.C: Weigh practical size against the cost before deciding
options.D: Re-run until the cost increase isn't significant

knowledge_check.why: Significant isn't the same as worth it.

parts.title: Diagnose system issues
parts.official_wording: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
parts.architecture_example: Extraction dropped on two document types right after an unevaluated move to a cheaper tier. That's model mismatch, fixed with per-type evals and routing.
parts.exam_takeaway: Classify the failure before fixing it. Grounding fixes hallucination, specification fixes prompt failure, and evals gate model choice.
parts.narration:
When something goes wrong, classify it before you fix it, because each class has a different cure.

A prompt failure means the instruction was ambiguous, and the model filled the gap differently each time. Output formats vary run to run. The fix is in the prompt: state the format, the constraints, and what to do when a field is missing.

A hallucination is confident, fluent content that isn't grounded in the source, like citations to papers that don't exist. Stronger wording won't fix it. Grounding will: retrieval, tools, and checking that each cited thing actually exists.

Model mismatch means the tier is wrong for the task, often after a swap without an eval. Look for category-specific drops right after the change.

And in multi-agent systems, use a shared trace to tell a recoverable subagent failure from an orchestrator failure.

Always start by asking what changed: the model version, the prompt, the corpus, or the mix of inputs. A RAG system that turns wrong right after a document refresh, with the model and latency unchanged, points at retrieval and indexing first.

knowledge_check.question: The same input gives differently structured outputs, and the prompt never specifies a format. Which class?

options.A: Hallucination
options.C: Prompt failure
options.D: Orchestrator failure

knowledge_check.why: Underspecification invites improvisation.

knowledge_check.question: The assistant cites journal articles that don't exist. What's the best fix?

options.A: Add an instruction to only cite real sources
options.B: Set the temperature to zero for every call
options.C: Switch to a larger model trained on more papers
options.D: Ground citations and verify they exist

knowledge_check.why: Hallucination needs grounding, not wording.

knowledge_check.question: Quality slid over weeks with no code change. What do you do first?

options.A: Check what changed and reproduce against the eval
options.B: Upgrade to the most capable model tier immediately
options.C: Rewrite the whole system prompt from scratch
options.D: Extend log retention so older data can be compared

knowledge_check.why: Attribute the cause before fixing.

parts.title: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
parts.official_wording: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
parts.architecture_example: Running Opus on every step cost seven times the plan. Tiering the classifier to Haiku and summaries to Sonnet, with Opus only for final composition, cut cost seventy-one percent with no change in satisfaction.
parts.exam_takeaway: Cache what's constant, tier each step, trim the context, and batch work that can wait. Model the token distribution, not the average.
parts.narration:
Optimising cost and latency means matching each lever to its driver.

If the same long prefix goes out on every call, cache it, with static content first. If the system runs one top-tier model everywhere, tier each step instead, proving each move with an eval. If context grows with every turn, switch to progressive context and compaction. If outputs run long, cap them and tighten the output contract. If thinking is switched on everywhere, keep it only where it measurably helps.

For bulk work that doesn't need an instant answer, like overnight reports, the Batch API trades waiting for a large discount. Check the current pricing, and confirm compliance coverage before sending regulated data through it.

Above all, build your cost model from the distribution of token usage, not the average. Most requests may be small, but a tail of long documents can account for most of the spend. One team found their long documents used eighty percent of the tokens, and an average-based estimate came in two to three times too low.

knowledge_check.question: Three hundred thousand descriptions needed by morning, with no interactive users. What fits?

options.A: Synchronous, at maximum concurrency
options.C: Top tier with thinking
options.D: Streaming

knowledge_check.why: Async work earns the batch discount.

knowledge_check.question: The bill is far above a forecast built on average tokens. Why?

options.A: The cache TTL was too short for reuse
options.B: Output tokens were priced as input
options.C: The model tier was assumed, not measured
options.D: The heavy-tailed distribution was ignored

knowledge_check.why: Model the distribution, not the average.

knowledge_check.question: Opus runs every step and cost is seven times plan. What's the approach?

options.A: Per-step evals and tiering
options.C: Add caching and change nothing else
options.D: Turn extended thinking on

knowledge_check.why: Tier each step to the cheapest model that passes.

parts.title: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
parts.official_wording: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
parts.architecture_example: A weekly eval re-run on sampled production traffic triggers an architect review after two consecutive weeks below threshold, even though error rate is flat.
parts.exam_takeaway: Monitor quality, not just uptime, and give every signal an owner and an action.
parts.narration:
Monitoring answers four questions. What is the system doing? How well? When did it change? And why?

Your dashboards should show cost per request, p50 and p95 latency, task success based on downstream acceptance, and errors by type. Make them breakable per request and per segment, because aggregate views can look healthy while a small slice of traffic burns the budget.

Threshold alerts catch sharp problems: a cost spike well above the weekly average, or p95 crossing the SLA. Slow quality drift won't trip those. For drift, re-run evals on sampled production traffic, and compare output distributions over time.

The people paying for the deployment don't read traces. Build a translation layer at design time that maps technical metrics to business ones, like task success to first-contact resolution, or latency to handle time. Then when the business asks whether it's working, you answer with a live query instead of a reconstruction.

And finally, a signal nobody owns changes nothing. Every alert needs a named owner and a defined action.

knowledge_check.question: Quality drifts slowly while error rate stays flat. What detects it?

options.A: A lower error-rate alert threshold
options.C: Scheduled evals and distribution comparison
options.D: Reading five transcripts every day by hand

knowledge_check.why: Drift needs periodic comparison.

knowledge_check.question: The sponsor asks about handle time, and dashboards only show latency and errors. What do you add?

options.A: A KPI translation layer
options.B: More latency percentiles on the dashboard
options.C: Direct access to the raw request logs
options.D: A weekly email of error counts

knowledge_check.why: Map technical metrics to business KPIs.

knowledge_check.question: Aggregates look fine, but cost is far over budget. What's missing?

options.A: A monthly cost review meeting
options.C: Longer log retention periods
options.D: Per-request decomposition

knowledge_check.why: Aggregates hide the expensive tail.

episodes.title: Episode 5 – Governance, Safety & Risk Management
episodes.intro: Episode five, Governance, Safety and Risk Management, is fourteen percent of the exam. Five parts: building guardrails, naming risks, routing decisions to humans, turning regulations into evidenced controls, and designing for fairness and transparency.

parts.title: Implement guardrails and safety controls
parts.official_wording: Implement guardrails and safety controls
key_concepts: input screening, output screening, tool authorization
parts.architecture_example: A refund agent's only guardrail was an output filter, which checked the text after the refund had already run. Deterministic authorization before the tool would have stopped it.
parts.exam_takeaway: Claude can't enforce a rule it was never given. Gate inputs, outputs and actions, and make each control fail closed.
parts.narration:
Claude arrives with broad safety behaviour built in. Anthropic trains it against a constitution that prioritises being broadly safe, ethical, compliant and genuinely helpful. That reduces broad harm. But training has never seen your partner's data rules or domain policy. If you assume it covers them, the rule goes unenforced everywhere.

So think in four layers. Trained behaviour, owned by Anthropic. The system prompt, which steers but doesn't enforce. Runtime screening. And authorization. You own the last three.

On the request path, there are three control points. Input screening, before the model call. Output screening, before the response reaches the user. And tool-call authorization, before any action with side effects. Authorization should be deterministic: an allowlist plus identity and scope. One filter at the end doesn't cover the other two points.

Decide what each control does when it errors. A guardrail that passes traffic when it fails gives the look of protection with none of the function. Fail closed.

Screen retrieved content and tool outputs as well, because that's where indirect injection arrives. And before installing third-party Skills, audit them, run them sandboxed with least privilege, and take them only from trusted sources.

knowledge_check.question: A domain policy was assumed to be covered by Claude's training. What's the result?

options.A: It's enforced by the constitution
options.B: It isn't enforced in any layer
options.C: Output screening covers it
options.D: It works on larger tiers

knowledge_check.why: Domain rules must live in a layer you build.

knowledge_check.question: The screening service times out and traffic passes. What should it do instead?

options.A: Fail open to keep traffic flowing
options.C: Fail closed and log
options.D: Switch off screening at peak hours

knowledge_check.why: A guardrail that fails open isn't protecting anything.

knowledge_check.question: Injected instructions arrive inside retrieved documents. What's the control?

options.A: Screen retrieved content before it enters context
options.C: Add a system-prompt rule to ignore such text
options.D: Lower top-k so fewer documents are retrieved

knowledge_check.why: Indirect injection bypasses user-input screening.

parts.title: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
parts.official_wording: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
key_concepts: walking the request and data paths
parts.architecture_example: A RAG and tools agent: screen uploaded PDFs for injection, cap input size and budgets, put an allowlist and recipient rule on send_email, and redact PII before logging.
parts.exam_takeaway: Walk every entry point, name the risk category, and record each one with a control, an owner and evidence.
parts.narration:
Most LLM risks fall into five categories. Direct prompt injection: a user tries to override the instructions. Indirect prompt injection: malicious instructions arrive through retrieved content or tool output. Token-budget exhaustion: huge or padded inputs that truncate work or inflate cost. Tool abuse: the model is induced to call a side-effecting tool outside policy. And data exposure: sensitive fields ending up in the context window or the logs.

On top of these sit the model's own limitations. It can be confidently wrong. Its knowledge can be stale. Its working memory has a hard edge. And it isn't deterministic. A demo that gives the same answer five times proves nothing about the sixth.

Failure modes also depend on the architecture. Agents run away on tool use and context. RAG drifts as the corpus changes. Document pipelines lack exception paths. Multi-agent systems drop units silently.

To assess a system, walk the request and data paths: user input, retrieved content, tool outputs, model output, and logs. At each point, ask what an attacker could do and what stops them. Then write it down. A written risk assessment, with a control, an owner and evidence for every risk, is what the security reviewer signs.

knowledge_check.question: Hidden instructions sit on a web page the agent reads. Which category?

options.A: Direct prompt injection
options.C: Token-budget exhaustion
options.D: Indirect injection

knowledge_check.why: The payload arrives through content the agent retrieves.

knowledge_check.question: Users paste giant padded logs, causing truncation and cost spikes. What's the control?

options.A: Input limits, max_tokens and per-turn budgets
options.B: Redact sensitive values from the logs
options.C: Add retrieval to ground the answers
options.D: Put authorization on the log tools

knowledge_check.why: Bound the budget to prevent exhaustion.

knowledge_check.question: What does a security reviewer sign off on?

options.A: The architecture diagram, annotated with data flows
options.B: A written risk assessment with controls, owners and evidence
options.C: The latest eval scores for quality and safety
options.D: A list of known limitations from public model docs

knowledge_check.why: The assessment is a deliverable.

parts.title: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
parts.official_wording: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
parts.architecture_example: A near-threshold benefits applicant with incomplete documents and a recommended deny goes to pre-action caseworker review, with the inputs and the flag reason shown.
parts.exam_takeaway: If it can't be undone and the system isn't sure, a person decides first. Route by stakes, not by volume.
parts.narration:
Think of human review as a budget. Reviewer attention is limited, so spend it where it matters most.

Two variables set the stakes: how reversible the decision is, and what a wrong decision would cost. A third, confidence, estimates how likely this particular output is to be wrong. But confidence only helps if it's calibrated against real outcomes, because a model can be confidently wrong.

The rule: route to a person when confidence is low and the decision is irreversible or expensive. Let confident, reversible, cheap decisions through.

Then choose where the person sits. Pre-action approval means nothing irreversible happens unreviewed, but it adds latency. Post-action audit keeps throughput high, but only suits reversible decisions. Sampled review monitors quality without guarding each individual case.

What the reviewer sees matters as much as what they're sent. Show the inputs, the output, and the reason the item was flagged.

And beware consent fatigue. If people are asked to approve dozens of times in a row, they stop reading. For agents, move review up to the plan and to exceptions, and let permissions bound everything else.

knowledge_check.question: A wrong denial would remove benefits, and confidence is low. Where does review go?

options.A: Post-action audit
options.C: No review above 0.6
options.D: Pre-action approval

knowledge_check.why: Irreversible, high-cost and uncertain means a human goes first.

knowledge_check.question: Reviewers see four hundred items a day with only an approve button. What two fixes?

options.A: Hire more reviewers and keep routing everything
options.B: Remove human review, since it's just approvals
options.C: Route by stakes, and show inputs and the flag reason
options.D: Give each reviewer a daily approval quota

knowledge_check.why: Fix both the volume and the missing context.

knowledge_check.question: What must be true before routing on a confidence score?

options.A: It's calibrated against outcomes
options.B: It's set above 0.95 for every decision
options.C: The model explains the score in its output
options.D: It's derived from the length of the response

knowledge_check.why: Uncalibrated confidence is unreliable.

parts.title: Ensure compliance with regulations
parts.official_wording: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
parts.architecture_example: A logging change started writing metadata to a second region. No one owned the residency control, so it surfaced only at audit. An owner, a data-flow record and scheduled checks would have caught it.
parts.exam_takeaway: A compliant route is a prerequisite, not proof. Each obligation needs a control, an owner and living evidence.
parts.narration:
Compliance works in two steps.

First, constraints remove options before anything else is decided. Attorney-client privilege rules out consumer tools and points to the API behind the firm's own gateway, with single sign-on and full logging. HIPAA requires a business associate agreement covering the specific configuration and features in use, and beta features are generally excluded. A requirement to keep data in the EU points, per the modules, to a cloud route pinned to an EU region. Government workloads need a route authorised at the required FedRAMP level. These specifics change, so always verify the current status.

Inside whatever route survives, minimise data. If the language task doesn't need a field, like a social security number, it shouldn't be in the context window, where it can land in application logs. Redact it on the server before the call.

Second, turn each obligation into a control register: the technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact a reviewer will accept, like a signed agreement, a configuration screen, or a live log query. A design document isn't evidence.

Revalidate on a schedule, because configurations drift. And don't confuse training use with retention. Data excluded from training may still be retained for other purposes.

knowledge_check.question: A healthcare partner has a BAA and wants to use a new beta feature. What do you verify?

options.A: Nothing more, since a BAA is already signed
options.B: That this configuration and feature are BAA-eligible
options.C: Only that data is encrypted in transit
options.D: Only that the feature is offered in-region

knowledge_check.why: Coverage is per configuration and feature.

knowledge_check.question: Social security numbers land in app logs although the task doesn't need them. What's the fix?

options.A: Encrypt the application logs at rest
options.B: Shorten log retention to seven days
options.C: Tell the model not to repeat identifiers
options.D: Redact on the server before the call

knowledge_check.why: Data minimisation keeps unneeded fields out of context.

knowledge_check.question: What does an auditor accept as proof that a control is operating?

options.A: A design document describing the control
options.B: An evidence artifact such as a configuration or a log query
options.C: The vendor's compliance marketing pages
options.D: An architecture diagram of the compliant route

knowledge_check.why: Proof means showing the control is live.

parts.title: Address ethical AI considerations
parts.official_wording: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
key_concepts: explanations for users, regulators and the team
parts.architecture_example: A team assumed fairness was the model vendor's job. The skew came from their retrieval corpus, and they had too little logging to prove it.
parts.exam_takeaway: Fairness enters at points you control. Instrument them, and log decisions well enough to explain any one of them.
parts.narration:
It's tempting to treat fairness as the model provider's problem. They trained the model and published bias evaluations, after all. But once you pair that model with your own data and logic, unequal outcomes can come in through four doors you control.

The retrieval corpus may over- or under-represent some groups. The prompt's framing may assume an answer. Few-shot examples may all show one kind of case. And downstream routing may send some groups down different paths.

So instrument each of those points, and measure outcomes by segment. An overall metric can look fine while harm concentrates in one subgroup.

Transparency means being able to explain any decision to three different audiences. An affected person needs a reason they can act on. A regulator needs evidence that comparable cases were treated consistently, and the ability to reconstruct a specific decision. Your team needs the full trace to debug it.

All three depend on decision logging: the inputs, the retrieved context, the output and the routing, kept so one decision can be replayed. Remember that the log is sensitive data itself, so minimise it, limit retention, and control access.
