knowledge_check.question: The model passed the vendor's bias evals, but outcomes are still unequal. Where do you look?

options.A: Only the vendor's original training data
options.B: Nowhere, since the vendor's evals settle it
options.C: System latency for different applicant groups
options.D: Corpus, prompt framing, examples and routing

knowledge_check.why: These are the injection points you control.

knowledge_check.question: A regulator asks you to reconstruct one adverse decision. What do you need?

options.A: Decision-level logs
options.C: The system prompt
options.D: Satisfaction scores

knowledge_check.why: Reconstruction needs per-decision records.

knowledge_check.question: Every few-shot example shows approvals from one region. What's the fix?

options.A: Add more examples from the same region
options.B: Phrase neutrally and balance the examples
options.C: Remove every example and go zero-shot
options.D: Switch to a larger, less biased model

knowledge_check.why: Unbalanced examples build bias into the prompt.

episodes.title: Episode 6 – Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
episodes.intro: Episode six covers stakeholder communication and lifecycle management, fourteen percent of the exam. Five parts: structured discovery, communicating trade-offs, feedback loops and SLAs, documentation that survives a handoff, and moving through the lifecycle. Partner-track demo and sales content is optional and not tested.

parts.title: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
parts.official_wording: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
key_concepts: must do, must not do, must cost, must prove
parts.architecture_example: "We want it to feel seamless" became a p95 latency target, no re-entering upstream data, exceptions routed quietly to a reviewer, and failures that never expose internals.
parts.exam_takeaway: A preference tells you to keep asking. Finish all four question buckets before you sketch anything.
parts.narration:
Discovery isn't a casual conversation. It's a structured elicitation with three steps: listen, translate, and write it down.

Translation is the core skill. Stakeholders speak in preferences: seamless, fast, simple. Designs are built against constraints. When you hear a preference, ask what would break it. What should the user never notice? What has to stay true when something fails? The answers become constraints you can test, like a latency target, a handoff rule, or a safe failure path.

Work through four buckets. What the system must do, as business outcomes. What it must not do: prohibited actions, and cases that must go to a person. What it must cost: budgets, latency, volume. And what it must prove: the evidence and audit obligations. Stakeholders rarely volunteer the last two, so ask for them directly.

Record each item as a row in a translation table: what was said, the constraint it implies, the architectural decision it forces, and any assumption still to confirm. Label assumptions clearly.

And watch for the classic trap. When an architect starts sketching mid-call, a confident design makes everyone assume the questions have been answered. Phrases like "it's just a quick review" often hide a mandatory approval step.

knowledge_check.question: A stakeholder says, "make it seamless". What's the next move?

options.A: Write "seamless" down as a requirement
options.C: Ask what would make it not seamless
options.D: Ask them to define it later

knowledge_check.why: Translate the preference into testable constraints.

knowledge_check.question: Which question buckets are stakeholders least likely to volunteer?

options.A: Must not do, and must prove
options.C: UI colours and project naming
options.D: Timelines and team staffing

knowledge_check.why: Boundaries and evidence obligations must be asked for.

knowledge_check.question: How should an unconfirmed item be recorded?

options.A: As a confirmed requirement in the spec
options.B: As a fact, since it seems obvious
options.C: Left out until someone raises it again
options.D: As a labelled assumption with an owner

knowledge_check.why: Unsourced assumptions are the most dangerous kind.

parts.title: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
parts.official_wording: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
key_concepts: Gain, give up, reversal cost, compliance posture
parts.architecture_example: A CTO approved "four cents a call" without hearing that, at production volume, it meant a five-figure monthly bill, or what unwinding the choice would cost. "I approved a direction, not a number."
parts.exam_takeaway: Present every trade-off with its gain, what it gives up, and what reversing it would cost, all in business terms.
parts.narration:
Your job in a decision meeting isn't to deliver a verdict. It's to make an informed decision possible.

Every option you present needs three elements. What it gains. What it gives up. And what reversing it would cost once the system has been built around it. In regulated settings, add a fourth: what it does to the compliance posture.

The reversal cost is the element people forget, and it's the one that changes the meeting. It turns "which is technically better?" into "which is the better business choice?"

Translate the numbers too. A per-call cost means little until you multiply it by real production volume and show the monthly total.

Present the decision as a package: the options you considered, the criteria, your recommendation, and the risks that remain. The stakeholder will have to defend this choice to their own leadership, so give them that justification.

Lead with the business outcome, not the architecture. And state limits honestly. A security stakeholder trusts a system whose limits are spelled out far more than one whose limits they discover later.

knowledge_check.question: Which trade-off element is most often missing?

options.A: The gain
options.C: The reversal cost
options.D: An architecture diagram

knowledge_check.why: It's what changes the decision.

knowledge_check.question: A CFO asks, "what happens if we choose wrong?" What do you do?

options.A: Explain it again with more technical detail
options.B: Defer the decision to the engineering team
options.C: Recommend the cheapest option to end the debate
options.D: Translate into business consequences, including reversal cost

knowledge_check.why: Stakeholders need consequences, not jargon.

knowledge_check.question: A sceptical security stakeholder is in the room. Which approach works best?

options.A: State limits and their controls honestly
options.C: Provide a sixty-page technical appendix
options.D: Promise the limits will be fixed next release

knowledge_check.why: Clearly stated limits build trust.

parts.title: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment, including SLAs
parts.official_wording: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
key_concepts: SLA as measure, breach and consequence
parts.architecture_example: An eval score drifted for seven weeks with no alert, because no rule tied slow drift to a trigger and an owner. A quarterly review finally caught it.
parts.exam_takeaway: Monitoring isn't a feedback loop. Every signal needs a trigger, an owner and an action, and some reviews run on a calendar.
parts.narration:
Observability tells you what the system is doing. A feedback loop decides what to do about it. It runs in five steps: signals, triage, decide, act, review.

Build it as a governance table before launch. Each row maps a signal, like eval score, p95 latency, cost per interaction, or data residency, to a review trigger, an owner and an action. Include slow drifts, not just hard failures. A score that sinks a little each week never trips an error alert.

An SLA names three things: what's measured, what counts as a breach, and what happens when one occurs. And every threshold should trace to something real. Latency to the user-experience expectation from discovery. Availability to how critical the business process is. Quality to your eval acceptance criteria.

Cost is the expectation that breaks most often after launch. Production volume can be ten to a hundred times the pilot. Give a forecast, and a spend-control plan, before the first invoice.

In regulated work, some reviews run on a schedule whether or not anything looks wrong, like periodic output audits or residency checks. Wire them in before launch.

knowledge_check.question: Eval scores drifted for weeks and no alert fired. What was missing?

options.A: More dashboards showing the same score
options.C: A governance rule tying drift to a trigger and owner
options.D: A larger eval dataset per category

knowledge_check.why: Signals need triggers and owners.

knowledge_check.question: Where should a latency SLA threshold come from?

options.A: The fastest result seen in load testing
options.C: A competitor's published response times
options.D: The model's documented maximum speed

knowledge_check.why: Thresholds trace to real sources.

knowledge_check.question: When does a periodic regulated output audit run?

options.A: On schedule, regardless of scores
options.B: Only when the eval score crosses a threshold
options.C: Only after an incident has been reported
options.D: Once, at the end of the contract term

knowledge_check.why: Some obligations are calendar-based.

parts.title: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
parts.official_wording: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
parts.architecture_example: A successor switched context strategies to fix performance and broke data residency, because the diagram showed what the system was but not why.
parts.exam_takeaway: Record why, and why not. The test is whether someone who wasn't in the room can make a safe change.
parts.narration:
Documentation is what keeps a design working after you've left. It serves three readers.

The engineer who inherits the system needs the decisions, plus the alternatives you rejected and why. Without those, they can't tell which choices are load-bearing. They may reverse the right decision for an understandable wrong reason.

The compliance reviewer needs each obligation mapped to its control, its owner, and current evidence. Statements that a control exists aren't enough.

And the architect who returns months later, maybe you, needs dated decisions, assumptions clearly labelled as assumptions, and open items with owners.

The completeness test is practical. Could a competent architect who wasn't in any of the design sessions read this and make a safe change? If not, it isn't done.

Two more artifacts belong here. For deployments spanning several entry points, an entry-point-responsibility map says which route owns which task and why, so tasks don't quietly drift onto the wrong route. And the outcome document records the business metric before and after, the auditable control, and the measurement owner.

knowledge_check.question: A successor broke residency by changing a load-bearing decision. What was missing?

options.A: A more detailed architecture diagram
options.B: More code comments in the repository
options.C: A list of team members and their roles
options.D: The rationale and rejected alternatives

knowledge_check.why: A diagram shows what, not why.

knowledge_check.question: What's the completeness test for documentation?

options.A: Whether it runs to over fifty pages
options.B: Whether the sponsor has signed it off
options.C: Whether an outsider can make a safe change
options.D: Whether every log line is included in it

knowledge_check.why: This is the safe-change test.

knowledge_check.question: Regulated data drifted onto the wrong route over time. Which artifact prevents this?

options.A: An entry-point-responsibility map
options.B: A larger eval set with regulated cases
options.C: Moving every task onto a single route
options.D: More logging on the direct-API path

knowledge_check.why: It makes route boundaries explicit.

parts.title: Support lifecycle phases
parts.official_wording: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
parts.architecture_example: A 529 overloaded error at peak took down a workflow that had no retries, no circuit breaker and no fallback. The demo had never shown any of these needs.
parts.exam_takeaway: A POC proves capability, nothing more. Know which phase you're in, and when monitoring should send you back to design.
parts.narration:
Every deployment moves through five phases: discovery, design, handoff, monitoring and iteration.

Discovery produces the translation table. Design produces the pattern, the sizing, the eval suite written before code, the feasibility verdict, the trade-off package and the control register. Handoff produces the decision log, the runbooks and the responsibility map. Monitoring runs the observability stack and the governance table. And iteration runs eval-gated changes and experiments.

The riskiest transition is from proof of concept to production. A POC runs at low volume, on clean inputs, with patient users. It proves the system can do the task. It tells you nothing about cost at scale, p95 latency under load, reliability, or how it fails on inputs nobody tested.

So before production, add the reliability controls, each at its own layer. Retries with exponential backoff close to the API call. Circuit breakers at the service boundary. Fallback chains in the orchestration layer. Pin model versions, and keep an update runbook.

And know when iteration isn't enough. If the constraints themselves change, like triple the volume or a new residency rule, go back to design.

knowledge_check.question: A POC worked perfectly at thirty requests a day. What does it prove?

options.A: Production readiness
options.C: Cost at scale
options.D: p95 under load

knowledge_check.why: Cost, latency, reliability and failure modes still need design.

knowledge_check.question: Where do retries with exponential backoff belong?

options.A: Near the API call
options.C: Only in orchestration
options.D: At the user interface

knowledge_check.why: Each reliability control works at its own layer.

knowledge_check.question: Volume tripled, and a residency rule arrived. What's the lifecycle move?

options.A: Keep tuning prompts
options.C: Drop the SLA
options.D: Re-architect

knowledge_check.why: Changed constraints send you back to design.

episodes.title: Episode 7 – Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
episodes.intro: Episode seven, Developer Productivity and Operational Enablement, is seven percent of the exam. Three parts: setting up Claude tooling for teams, improving developer workflows without lowering the quality bar, and supporting operations so the team can solve problems on its own.

parts.title: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams
parts.official_wording: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
parts.architecture_example: A release-notes Skill shipped as a flat bundle with no versioning. One bad edit broke output for forty engineers. A group-assigned plugin with versioned updates would have allowed a rollback.
parts.exam_takeaway: Give every developer the same baseline, roll out through champions, govern shared Skills through plugins, and set spend limits before the first bill.
parts.narration:
Configuring Claude for yourself takes minutes. Configuring it for a team means four deliberate decisions.

First, a shared configuration. The team agrees one baseline, with a project CLAUDE.md, an agreed set of tools and MCP servers, and a permission posture, so nobody starts from their own drifting setup.

Second, the rollout. Don't switch everyone on at once. Enable one champion per department, let them prove a real workflow, then spread adoption batch by batch.

Third, how Skills reach people. Organisation-provisioned Skills reach everyone, but have no native rollback. Plugins assigned to a group give you targeting, install preferences and versioned updates from a repository, the strongest governance. Project Skills live in the repository and version with it. API Skills are called by your own products, with version pinning.

Fourth, the spend posture: model defaults, allowlists, effort guidance, and spend and rate caps.

Inside Claude Code, separate the layers that shape behaviour, like CLAUDE.md, Skills, subagents and MCP, from the layers that govern it: hooks, permission modes and sandboxing. If something must always happen, use a hook. An instruction is not a guarantee.

knowledge_check.question: How should Claude Code be rolled out across four departments?

options.A: Enable everyone at once by email
options.C: Champions first, then batches
options.D: Wait until a full curriculum exists

knowledge_check.why: Champions absorb friction and seed adoption.

knowledge_check.question: Which distribution supports group targeting and rollback?

options.A: A plugin with versioned updates
options.C: Skill files emailed to each engineer
options.D: Procedures pasted into every prompt

knowledge_check.why: Plugins give the strongest governance.

knowledge_check.question: A linter must always run before commits. Which layer?

options.A: A CLAUDE.md line
options.C: A subagent
options.D: A hook

knowledge_check.why: Hooks are deterministic gates.

parts.title: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
parts.official_wording: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
parts.architecture_example: Generated code passed review and tests, then leaked data through an input it never validated. The author couldn't explain the code.
parts.exam_takeaway: AI-generated code meets the same bar as hand-written code, and the person merging it must understand it.
parts.narration:
AI tooling pays off when it lives inside the workflow developers already use: the editor, code review, and the test loop. Not in a separate chat window they visit now and then. Encode team conventions and review standards as Skills and project configuration, so good practice travels with the tooling.

Claude helps at each stage. Writing: boilerplate, tests and first drafts from a clear spec. Reviewing: summarising diffs and flagging likely issues. Debugging: suggesting hypotheses from a symptom and a trace. But each stage still needs human discipline. Flags are input, not a verdict. Hypotheses get checked against evidence.

Two adoption failures come up again and again. Lumpy adoption, where a few people use the tool heavily and everyone else barely does. And stalling at chat, where the team never moves past asking questions to tool use and repository-aware help.

The safeguard is diligence, turned into a verification checklist: correctness, security, maintainability, and human understanding. Automate whatever you can with tests and evals. And keep one question non-negotiable: can the person merging this explain what it does and why?

knowledge_check.question: Generated code shipped and no one could explain it. What was missing?

options.A: More AI review tools on each pull request
options.B: A verification checklist that includes human understanding
options.C: A faster CI pipeline to catch issues sooner
options.D: A bigger code-generation model with fewer bugs

knowledge_check.why: Speed mustn't replace understanding.

knowledge_check.question: Three of forty developers use Claude, and the rest only chat. Which failures?

options.A: Over-adoption by a few heavy users
options.B: Model mismatch on the chosen tier
options.C: Lumpy adoption and stalling at chat
options.D: A cost overrun from unmanaged usage

knowledge_check.why: Access isn't adoption.

knowledge_check.question: How should reviewers treat a Claude "no issues found" flag?

options.A: As input, with the human making the call
options.B: As authoritative, so reviewers save time
options.C: Disable AI review, since people over-rely on it
options.D: Run it on weekends only, for low-risk changes

knowledge_check.why: AI flags are input, not a verdict.

parts.title: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
parts.official_wording: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
parts.architecture_example: Answer quality slid for a whole quarter because a growing retrieval corpus outpaced the index. A runbook entry for "gradual decline, no code change" would have pointed straight to retrieval drift.
parts.exam_takeaway: Connect the symptom to its cause, fix it once, write it down, and teach the team the path.
parts.narration:
When a live deployment surprises its team, they usually see a symptom, not a cause. The architect's job is to connect the two, and then teach the team how to do it next time.

A few patterns cover most cases. Quality declining slowly with no code change points to a model or prompt change, or to retrieval drift as the corpus grows. Compare against the eval set and check what changed. A latency spike usually means context grew, a tool slowed down, or the cache stopped hitting, so find the slowest span in the trace. Intermittent tool failures point to authorization, rate limits or an unhandled error, so trace one failed call from end to end. And cost rising while usage stays flat means the model tier crept up or caching broke.

For transient errors, like rate limits, timeouts and overload responses, retry with exponential backoff. Don't retry requests that were simply invalid.

Then make the fix last. Write a runbook entry mapping the symptom to the cause and the first action. Define an escalation path: who handles what, and when an issue leaves the team. The goal is a team that only needs you for problems nobody has seen before.

knowledge_check.question: Cost rose sixty percent with flat traffic. What do you check first?

options.A: Network latency to the API endpoint
options.B: Recent changes to the prompt's tone
options.C: How many developers now use Claude Code
options.D: Per-request model tier and cache hit rate

knowledge_check.why: Tier creep or a caching regression is likely.

knowledge_check.question: Tool calls fail mostly at peak. What's the first diagnostic step?

options.A: Switch to a more capable model tier
options.B: Rewrite the system prompt for tool use
options.C: Trace one failed call end to end
options.D: Increase the context window size

knowledge_check.why: Check authorization, rate limits and error paths.

knowledge_check.question: What makes an operational fix durable?

options.A: The architect watching quality personally
options.B: A runbook entry plus an escalation path
options.C: Blindly re-indexing the corpus each month
options.D: Refreshing the dashboards more often

knowledge_check.why: This builds team self-sufficiency.
